card.chief_complaint: new confusion and low blood pressure

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.rationale: Recent medication changes or antihypertensives could explain hypotension and guide immediate management.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop or taper the culprit and check sodium; the review is additive to, not a replacement for, the infectious/metabolic delirium workup.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not delay sepsis, hypoglycemia or stroke evaluation while the medication list is being reconciled.
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt benzodiazepine or opioid withdrawal can itself cause delirium, seizures or severe pain; taper rather than stop in chronic users.
ask.how: Reconcile every current drug (including OTC, PRN and recently stopped) against the admission list and the last 72 h MAR. Flag anticholinergics, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, opioids, dihydropyridines, antihistamines, steroids, any drug added or dose-changed in the past week, and diuretics/thiazides (sodium).
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug identified does not exclude delirium or medication effect; look for infection, metabolic and structural causes.
ask.pitfalls: Risk data are relative risks/odds ratios from cohort studies, not diagnostic sensitivity or specificity, so no LR can be assigned. Untreated severe pain also precipitates delirium, so opioids should be tapered rather than abruptly withdrawn.
ask.positive_finding: One or more deliriogenic drugs or a recent addition/dose change temporally preceding the mental-status change. More than three drugs added during admission roughly triples delirium risk in older inpatients.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable medication history from chart, pharmacy record or family; time of each new start or dose change.
ask.rationale: Identifying deliriogenic medications is crucial in a newly confused, post-op patient to guide withdrawal or adjustment.
ask.title: Deliriogenic medication review: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, new/changed drugs, thiazides

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: The value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Adults with clinically suspected DVT in cohort studies
evidence.quote: it stratified patients into groups with high (LR, 5.2), intermediate, and low (LR, 0.25) probability of DVT
evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis (imaging-confirmed), Wells score high vs low category

evidence.citation: Wells PS, Owen C, Doucette S, Fergusson D, Tran H. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 2006;295(2):199-207.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results (post-test prevalence by Wells category; no sens/spec/LR)
evidence.population: Consecutive unselected outpatients with suspected DVT, 14 studies (>8000 patients)
evidence.quote: prevalence of DVT in the low, moderate, and high clinical probability groups was 5.0% (95% CI, 4.0%-8.0%), 17% (95% CI, 13%-23%), and 53%
evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis, prevalence by Wells clinical probability category

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: Recent surgery and immobilization increase VTE risk, which could present as shock or confusion post-operatively.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: A positive survey targets cultures, imaging and source control (line removal, drainage, debridement); a negative survey mandates blood/urine cultures and imaging rather than reassurance.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay cultures and antibiotics in suspected sepsis while completing the survey.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never let a negative source survey withhold cultures, empiric antibiotics or imaging in a hypotensive, febrile or acutely confused patient with suspected infection.
examine.escalation_warning: Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion (necrotizing fasciitis), a hot joint, peritonism, or purulence at a central line/dialysis catheter in a septic patient require immediate surgical/source-control and line removal decisions.
examine.how: Undress and inspect every line, dialysis and drain/exit site (erythema, purulence, tunnel tenderness), all skin including back, sacrum, heels, perineum, injection sites and wounds; palpate abdomen (peritonism, Murphy sign, flank tenderness), joints and spine for warmth/effusion/tenderness; check urinary catheter, mouth, sinuses, ears and chest. Repeat daily while the source is unknown.
examine.negative_finding: A normal survey does not exclude an occult source: insertion-site inflammation is absent in nearly all catheter-related bloodstream infections, and intra-abdominal, urinary, endovascular and spinal infections are frequently silent in elderly, immunosuppressed or sedated patients.
examine.pitfalls: Line-site appearance has near-zero sensitivity for CRBSI (coagulase-negative staphylococci cause little inflammation); steroids, neutropenia and neuropathy blunt local signs; dressings, obesity and immobility hide sacral, perineal and injection-site infections. Pain out of proportion with unimpressive skin findings suggests necrotizing infection.
examine.positive_finding: Purulence, spreading erythema or tunnel tenderness at a line/exit site, cellulitis or crepitus, a hot swollen joint, peritonism or flank tenderness, or a sacral/heel ulcer with surrounding infection identifies a probable source and directs cultures, source control and empiric therapy.
examine.prerequisites: Full exposure with dressings taken down, adequate lighting and analgesia; review lines, catheters and devices with their insertion dates; log-roll immobile patients to view the sacrum.
examine.rationale: A focused infection source exam is essential in a post-op, hypotensive, confused patient to identify treatable septic foci.
examine.title: Focused infection-source exam (line/exit sites, skin, abdomen, joints, sacrum, urine catheter)

examine.changes_what: Elevated SI: escalate to resuscitation, early lactate, source/bleeding search and transfusion readiness; normal SI: do not de-escalate on this alone.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on SI in patients on beta-blockers or with pacemakers, in pregnancy beyond the first trimester, or in children (use age-adjusted SIPA).
examine.escalation_warning: SI >=1.0 with a bleeding source, suspected AAA, PE or infection indicates shock and warrants immediate resuscitation, senior review and ICU-level care.

evidence.citation: DeMuro JP, Simmons S, Jax J, Gianelli SM. Application of the Shock Index to the prediction of need for hemostasis intervention. Am J Emerg Med. 2013.
evidence.population: 4277 adult (>16 y) trauma patients at a single trauma centre over 11 years; traumatic brain injury and transfers excluded; retrospective
evidence.quote: using the standard SI cutoff of >0.9 as the threshold for bleeding, the sensitivity is 54.5%, with a specificity of 93.6%
evidence.reference_standard: Bleeding requiring intervention for hemostasis (study definition; the Koch 2019 review summarises it as >=2 units PRBC in 24 h)
evidence.target_condition: PROGNOSTIC: Hemorrhage requiring hemostasis intervention after trauma — SI >0.9 (initial hospital vitals)

evidence.citation: DeMuro JP, Simmons S, Jax J, Gianelli SM. Application of the Shock Index to the prediction of need for hemostasis intervention. Am J Emerg Med. 2013.
evidence.population: 4277 adult (>16 y) trauma patients at a single trauma centre over 11 years; traumatic brain injury and transfers excluded; retrospective
evidence.quote: Lowering the SI to ≥0.8 increases the sensitivity to 76.1%, with a specificity of 87.4%
evidence.reference_standard: Bleeding requiring intervention for hemostasis (study definition; the Koch 2019 review summarises it as >=2 units PRBC in 24 h)
evidence.target_condition: PROGNOSTIC: Hemorrhage requiring hemostasis intervention after trauma — SI >=0.8 (lowered threshold)

evidence.citation: Berger T, Green J, Horeczko T, Hagar Y, Garg N, Suarez A, Panacek E, Shapiro N. Shock index and early recognition of sepsis in the emergency department: pilot study. West J Emerg Med. 2013.
evidence.location: Full text (PMC), Table 3 'Performance of predictors for hyperlactatemia', column SI ≥ 1.0
evidence.population: 2524 adult ED patients with suspected infection screened for severe sepsis; retrospective; hyperlactatemia in 290 (11.5%)
evidence.reference_standard: Initial serum lactate >=4.0 mmol/L (hyperlactatemia as surrogate for severe sepsis)
evidence.target_condition: Hyperlactatemia (lactate >=4.0 mmol/L) in ED patients with suspected infection — SI >=1.0 at triage

evidence.citation: Berger T, Green J, Horeczko T, Hagar Y, Garg N, Suarez A, Panacek E, Shapiro N. Shock index and early recognition of sepsis in the emergency department: pilot study. West J Emerg Med. 2013.
evidence.location: Full text (PMC), Table 3 'Performance of predictors for hyperlactatemia', column SI ≥ 0.7
evidence.population: 2524 adult ED patients with suspected infection screened for severe sepsis; retrospective; hyperlactatemia in 290 (11.5%)
evidence.reference_standard: Initial serum lactate >=4.0 mmol/L (hyperlactatemia as surrogate for severe sepsis)
evidence.target_condition: Hyperlactatemia (lactate >=4.0 mmol/L) in ED patients with suspected infection — SI >=0.7 at triage

evidence.citation: Birkhahn RH, Gaeta TJ, Van Deusen SK, Tloczkowski J. The ability of traditional vital signs and shock index to identify ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2003.
evidence.population: 52 ED patients with ectopic pregnancy (25 ruptured, 27 unruptured); retrospective case-control
evidence.quote: sensitivity for heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and heart rate/systolic blood pressure was 28%, 36%, and 72% respectively; the specificity was 96%, 96%, and 67%
evidence.target_condition: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy (hemoperitoneum) — SI (HR/SBP) >0.7 at presentation; case-control design

examine.how: Divide the heart rate (beats/min) by the systolic blood pressure (mmHg) from the first set of triage vital signs; normal is roughly 0.5-0.7. Record the threshold used (>0.9 or >=1.0) and recalculate with each new set of vitals to follow the trend.
examine.negative_finding: A normal SI does not exclude bleeding or sepsis (sensitivity 55% for hemorrhage at >0.9; 48% for lactate >=4 at >=1.0); lowering the threshold to 0.7-0.8 improves sensitivity at the cost of specificity.
examine.pitfalls: Beta-blockade, pacing, hypertension and age blunt the index; pain, anxiety, fever, and anemia raise it without shock. A single value is less informative than the trend.
examine.positive_finding: SI >0.9 in trauma has specificity ~94% for hemorrhage needing hemostasis (LR+ ~8.5 computed) and SI >=1.0 in suspected infection is the most specific vital-sign predictor of hyperlactatemia (spec 0.81); an elevated SI flags occult shock when HR and SBP each look acceptable.
examine.prerequisites: Accurate HR and SBP; note beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, pacemakers and baseline hypertension.
examine.rationale: Shock index helps rapidly identify severity and need for urgent resuscitation in hypotensive patients.
examine.title: Shock index (HR / SBP >= 0.9-1.0)

examine.changes_what: Prolonged CRT in shock: treat as ongoing hypoperfusion and reassess after resuscitation; normal CRT does not rule out hypovolemia.
examine.contraindications: Not interpretable on a cold, cyanotic or vasoconstricted limb, with peripheral arterial disease, or in the presence of nail polish/false nails.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use CRT to exclude hypovolemia or bleeding in adults; do not interpret on cold, vasoconstricted or peripherally diseased limbs.
examine.escalation_warning: Persistently prolonged CRT after initial resuscitation in septic shock marks a high-mortality group and should prompt reassessment of perfusion and escalation, not reassurance.

evidence.citation: Schriger DL, Baraff LJ. Capillary refill--is it a useful predictor of hypovolemic states? Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(6):601-605.
evidence.population: 13 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and hypotension; comparison group blood donors
evidence.quote: 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical hypovolemia group assignment (hypotension); age-sex specific CRT upper limit of normal
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (ED patients with suggestive history and frank hypotension)

evidence.citation: Schriger DL, Baraff LJ. Capillary refill--is it a useful predictor of hypovolemic states? Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(6):601-605.
evidence.population: 19 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and abnormal orthostatic vital signs
evidence.quote: 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical hypovolemia group assignment (abnormal orthostatics); age-sex specific CRT upper limit of normal
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (ED patients with suggestive history and abnormal orthostatic vital signs)

evidence.citation: Ait-Oufella H, Bige N, Boelle PY, et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive Care Med. 2014;40(7):958-964.
evidence.population: 59 consecutive adults with septic shock, tertiary ICU
evidence.quote: index CRT at 2.4 s predicted 14-day outcome with a sensitivity of 82% (95% CI [60-95]) and a specificity of 73% (95% CI [56-86])
evidence.target_condition: 14-day mortality after initial resuscitation of septic shock (index fingertip CRT >2.4 s at 6 h)

evidence.citation: Ait-Oufella H, Bige N, Boelle PY, et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive Care Med. 2014;40(7):958-964.
evidence.population: 59 consecutive adults with septic shock, tertiary ICU
evidence.quote: knee CRT at 4.9 s predicted 14-day outcome with a sensitivity of 82% (95% CI [60-95]) and a specificity of 84% (95% CI [68-94])
evidence.target_condition: 14-day mortality after initial resuscitation of septic shock (knee CRT >4.9 s at 6 h)

evidence.citation: Jacquet-Lagreze M, Wiart C, Schweizer R, et al. Prognostic value of capillary refill time in adult patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):473.
evidence.population: Adults with acute circulatory failure; 13 studies in primary analysis (23 studies, 60,656 patients overall)
evidence.quote: pooled sensitivity was 54% (95%CI [43; 64]). The pooled specificity was 72% (95%CI [55; 84])
evidence.reference_standard: Mortality as reported by each study
evidence.target_condition: Death in adults with acute circulatory failure (abnormal CRT, study-specific thresholds)

examine.how: With the hand at heart level in a warm room, press the distal index finger pad (or nail bed) firmly for 10-15 s until blanched, release, and time return of baseline colour with a watch. Prolonged is >3 s (ICU studies use >2.4-3 s at the fingertip; knee CRT is an alternative site).
examine.negative_finding: A normal CRT does not exclude mild-to-moderate hypovolemia in adults (sensitivity 6% after 450 mL loss). In acute circulatory failure, normal CRT only weakly lowers mortality risk (pooled LR- about 0.6).
examine.pitfalls: Cold room, cold hands, age and vasoconstriction prolong CRT without hypoperfusion; measurement quality (site, pressure, timing) strongly affects accuracy. CRT is a prognostic/perfusion marker, not a diagnostic test for the cause of shock.
examine.positive_finding: In resuscitated septic shock, a fingertip CRT >2.4 s at 6 h predicts 14-day death with sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%, and marks persisting hypoperfusion. In undifferentiated adults, a prolonged CRT is a weak sign of hypovolemia (sensitivity 26-46%).
examine.prerequisites: Warm extremity and ambient temperature; a second hand or watch to time; consistent pressure (a glass slide can standardise blanching).
examine.rationale: Prolonged capillary refill time indicates ongoing hypoperfusion and need for immediate intervention.
examine.title: Capillary refill time prolonged (>2-3 s, fingertip at heart level, warm room)

examine.changes_what: Positive: label as delirium and work up precipitants; negative: pursue dementia, depression, psychosis or focal neurology but rescreen if course fluctuates.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for glucose, vitals, and focal neurological exam in acute mental-status change; use CAM-ICU in ventilated or non-verbal patients.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive CAM with fever, meningism, focal deficit or reduced consciousness needs urgent evaluation for meningitis, stroke or sepsis regardless of screen result.

evidence.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Simel DL, Straus SE. Does this patient have delirium?: value of bedside instruments. JAMA 2010;304:779-786.
evidence.population: Hospitalized adults, mostly older medical/surgical inpatients, across 25 prospective studies (N=3027)
evidence.quote: the CAM has the best available supportive data as a bedside delirium instrument (summary-positive LR, 9.6; 95% CI, 5.8-16.0; summary-negative LR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.09-0.29)
evidence.reference_standard: DSM-based diagnosis by geriatrician, psychiatrist or neurologist

evidence.citation: Shi Q, Warren L, Saposnik G, Macdermid JC. Confusion assessment method: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy. Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2013;9:1359-1370.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results; Results text and Figure 2 (bivariate estimate)
evidence.population: Adults in a variety of medical settings; 22 studies of CAM and CAM-ICU (n=2442)
evidence.quote: The pooled sensitivities and specificity for CAM were 82% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 69%-91%) and 99% (95% CI: 87%-100%)

examine.how: After a brief cognitive test (e.g. months backwards, digit span) and interview, score four features: (1) acute onset and fluctuating course from an informant/chart, (2) inattention, (3) disorganized thinking, (4) altered level of consciousness. CAM positive = features 1 AND 2 plus either 3 or 4. Takes about 5 minutes.
examine.negative_finding: Negative CAM lowers the probability substantially (pooled LR- 0.16) but pooled sensitivity is only ~0.82; repeat the screen if fluctuation is suspected.
examine.pitfalls: Accuracy falls with untrained raters and without a formal attention test; dementia, aphasia and hypoactive delirium lower sensitivity. The CAM identifies delirium, not its cause.
examine.positive_finding: Positive CAM makes delirium roughly 10 times more likely (pooled LR+ 9.6) and should trigger a search for the precipitant (infection, drugs, metabolic, withdrawal).
examine.prerequisites: Baseline cognition from a collateral source; trained rater; patient able to respond (use CAM-ICU for intubated/non-verbal patients).
examine.rationale: A CAM screen will confirm delirium and prompt a focused search for reversible causes in this acutely confused patient.
examine.title: Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) delirium screen
